blindSummary:
Nothing about gender expression is criminalised here, but the country has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid a broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

The capital has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.
blindOutOfScope: General humanitarian and repression context affects all travellers; only the trans-specific protection vacuum is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: An LGBTQ news outlet (Sep 2024): reports LGBTQ people in this country facing unprecedented persecution after the disputed election, including detention and abuse.
A regional asylum agency's country-focus report, section 3.5: covers the situation of LGBTIQ+ persons in this country.
NOTE: an international LGBTQ-rights foundation's guide on this country (Oct 2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

A foreign broadsheet with a news agency (Aug 2015): this country's first transgender legislative candidate registered to stand for the legislature under a masculine birth name because the law does not allow legal gender change despite her 2002 surgery; she argued that this country, with several regional peers, has done little for equal rights.

National news site (March 2023): a polling firm's survey found 76% of residents support LGBTIQ people being open about their sexual orientation and gender identity - majority public support for equal rights.

Activist blog (Jan 2014): asking whether equal marriage is coming soon here - the sex/gender diversity community presented a bill for equal civil marriage amending the civil code's marriage provision; recalls the supreme court's 2008 ruling that the constitution does not discriminate on sexual orientation.

National newspaper (Dec 2015): an international human-rights organisation declared an openly gay deputy-elect and activist - founder of the advocacy group that first requested same-sex marriage in the legislature - a prisoner of conscience, held by the state intelligence service; he became the country's first openly gay parliamentarian.
blindLocalsOnly: The degraded healthcare including HRT access is resident-facing; the post-2024 persecution wave primarily affects resident activists and communities.
